slides.title: Was *BSEG* ever one table?

slides.label: WHY

slides.heading: The *3 types*
slides.voiceover: Transparent: one table in SE11 is one table in the database. Same name, same fields. Pooled: many small tables share one database table, the table pool. Cluster: related tables share one table cluster. Today, in S four hana, nearly all are transparent.

slides.spoken: Here's an example. In ECC, BSEG held your accounting items. It lived inside the cluster RFBLG. In S/4HANA, BSEG is transparent. VBAK, the sales order header, was always transparent.

slides.body: One table in SE11 = one table in the database. Pooled and cluster are mostly history.

slides.title: Delivery class *A or C*?
slides.voiceover: Stop treating all seven delivery classes the same. Last time we learned how to create a table. Now, the delivery class.
slides.spoken: Stop treating all 7 delivery classes the same. Last time we learned how to create a table. Now, the delivery class.

slides.label: NEW TERM
slides.heading: Who owns *the data*?
slides.body: Delivery class = who maintains the data, and how transports and client copies treat it.
slides.voiceover: Why does it matter? The delivery class says who maintains a table's data. And how transports and client copies treat it.
slides.spoken: Why does it matter? The delivery class says who maintains a table's data. And how transports and client copies treat it.

slides.heading: Where it *lives*
slides.voiceover: Open your table in SE11. Go to the Delivery and Maintenance tab. Delivery class is mandatory. Press F4 to see all seven.
slides.spoken: Open your table in SE11. Go to the Delivery and Maintenance tab. Delivery class is mandatory. Press F4 to see all 7.

slides.heading: The two you'll *use*
slides.voiceover: Application data is class A. Orders and customers, created by users in each system. Customizing is class C. Settings you transport from development to production.
slides.spoken: Application data is class A. Orders and customers, created by users in each system. Customizing is class C. Settings you transport from development to production.

slides.label: THE REST
slides.heading: The other *five*
slides.title: Delivery Class (F4)
slides.voiceover: Now the other five, quickly, one line each. L, temporary data. G, protected customizing, SAP only adds rows. E, control tables, with separate key areas. S, system tables only SAP maintains. W, system tables with their own transport objects.
slides.spoken: Now the other five, quickly, one line each. L, temporary data. G, protected customizing, SAP only adds rows. E, control tables, with separate key areas. S, system tables only SAP maintains. W, system tables with their own transport objects.

slides.label: EXAMPLE
slides.heading: Real *tables*
slides.title: Delivery class of real tables
slides.voiceover: Real examples. VBAK, the sales order header, is class A. T zero zero one, company codes, is class C.
slides.spoken: Real examples. VBAK, the sales order header, is class A. T001, company codes, is class C.

slides.label: COMMON MISTAKE
slides.heading: Settings in *class A*
slides.voiceover: Common mistake: class A for a settings table. Then your settings don't travel with a transport. Use C for settings.
slides.spoken: Common mistake: class A for a settings table. Then your settings don't travel with a transport. Use C for settings.

slides.label: REMEMBER
slides.heading: *A* = data, *C* = settings
slides.body: Pick the class by who owns the rows: users (A) or customizing (C).
slides.voiceover: Takeaway: A for business data, C for settings.
slides.spoken: Takeaway: A for business data, C for settings.
